prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, February, Undivided

outputs.L1:
The deer racing across a field  
of the same clay and tallow color  
they are—if they are:  
or are they tricks of the light?—  
must feel themselves being poured  
and pouring through life.

We’re not built  
but become: trembling columns  
of apprehension that ripple  
and pass those ripples to and fro  
with the world that shakes around us—  
it, too, is something poured  
and ceaselessly pouring itself.

February shakes the fields  
and trembles in each yellow willow.

•

The violin’s back is not veneer—  
the strummed wood shudders together.  
Undivided by caution,  
each note is its own first thought.

My first thought’s a kind of prayer  
that I might resonate entire—  
sometimes it’s such a meager portion,  
shaking a little, as if it ought...

Every day, the same desire  
to push myself through the door  
that leads to some bright place,  
brighter than the concert platform,  
where the whole self echoes together—  
the outer to the inner pleasure.

•

Everything runs together—  
the light smells of spring,  
the unreasonable brightness  
of this peg, this sheet, this line tethering  
linen between sky and mud,  
as if the garden marked a pause  
in that eternal return  
whose looping trace is the blood  
hissing through the ventricles.

What gives you life’s the thing that kills.
outputs.L2:
Deer sprint over a meadow that seems to share their hue—clay mixed with tallow—assuming they are truly there and not merely illusions made by light. Perhaps they experience existence as both liquid and motion, as though life streams into them while they stream through it. We are not finished structures; we are continually forming—quivering pillars of awareness, exchanging waves of sensation with a world that trembles in return, a world forever spilling outward and remaking itself. February sets the land vibrating, and every golden willow quivers with it.

•

The violin’s rear surface is solid wood, not a thin decorative layer; when the strings are played, the whole instrument trembles as one. Free from hesitation, every note arrives like an entirely new idea. My own earliest impulse resembles a prayer: may every part of me sound together. Yet sometimes only a frail fragment responds, faintly shaking, as though it knows it should do more. Each day brings back the same longing—to force myself across the threshold into a radiant place, more luminous than any stage, where my complete being reverberates in unity and inward delight answers outward sensation.

•

All things merge. The light carries spring’s scent. There is a strange intensity in the brightness of this clothespin, this fabric, this cord holding linen between earth’s muck and the open sky. The garden appears to interrupt the everlasting cycle for a moment, though that cycle’s circling pattern continues in the blood rushing through the heart’s chambers. The force that sustains life is also what ultimately destroys it.
outputs.L3:
The deer racing across the field seem almost to dissolve into the landscape. Their movement blurs the boundary between animal and environment, as though both are being continuously poured into existence. This image suggests that living beings are not fixed or self-contained. Instead, they are always becoming, exchanging tremors, rhythms, and ripples with the unstable world around them.

The image of the violin develops this idea through sound. When the instrument is played, its wood resonates as a unified whole rather than as a collection of separate parts. This complete response symbolizes the speaker’s desire to meet life with an equally integrated self—to feel and answer the world with every part of their being. The speaker longs to enter a brighter state of existence in which inner emotion and outer experience echo one another in perfect harmony.

Yet this vision of unity is not simply comforting. Everything blends within life’s recurring cycles of growth, transformation, decay, and renewal. The forces that animate the deer, awaken the violin’s music, and sustain the natural world are also the forces that eventually lead all living things toward death. Life and death are therefore not presented as opposites but as inseparable parts of the same continuous process.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents life not as a fixed state but as an ongoing process of transformation, movement, and vibration. Its images repeatedly cross the boundaries between the human body, the natural world, music, and perception. Running deer embody instinctive vitality, while trembling fields suggest that the landscape itself is alive and responsive. The resonant wood of a violin turns matter into sound, showing how physical substance can be transformed into emotion and meaning. Similarly, the bright garden becomes more than a visual scene: it is a space where light, growth, sensation, and consciousness meet.

Through these connections, the poem suggests that no living thing exists in isolation. Bodies move through nature, nature enters perception, and music reveals the hidden vibrations shared by all forms of matter. Life is therefore portrayed as a continuous circulation in which energy passes from one form to another. Yet this vitality cannot be separated from mortality. Growth contains the possibility of decay, movement tends toward stillness, and every living form is temporary. Rather than treating death as the opposite of life, the poem places both within the same flowing cycle.

Its conclusion embraces this paradox. Wholeness does not come from escaping change or denying mortality, but from becoming fully receptive to the rhythms that unite creation and dissolution. To live completely is to resonate—like the violin’s wood—with the forces passing through the body and the world. In that resonance, vitality and mortality are recognized as inseparable aspects of a single, continually transforming existence.
outputs.L5:
### The February Undivided

February arrived quietly, carrying snow in its pockets and a pale silver sky. Though it was the shortest month, its days felt full—each one bound to the next by frost, memory, and expectation.

In the stillness, the town seemed undivided. Footprints crossed the same white streets, warm lights glowed behind every window, and strangers exchanged smiles against the cold. For a brief season, differences softened beneath the snow.

It was February undivided: winter and spring, darkness and light, endings and beginnings—all held together in a single, fragile month.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a three-part free-verse poem about deer, a violin, and a garden, linked by images of trembling, resonance, and the fluid nature of existence.
counterfactuals.output:
### I. Deer

At the tree line,  
a deer lifts her head—

the whole meadow trembling  
inside one listening ear.

Morning slips across her back  
like water over stone.  
For a breath, she is there;  
for another, only grass  
remembering where she stood.

### II. Violin

The bow touches the string  
and finds a hidden river.

Wood shivers into song;  
the room becomes a body  
holding one long note.

Even silence resonates—  
a dark instrument  
passed from hand to hand,  
its shape changing  
with every touch.

### III. Garden

Rain loosens the garden  
from its names.

Rose, root, snail, soil—  
all flow into one another  
beneath the trembling leaves.

A drop hangs from a stem,  
round as a listening world,  
then falls.

The earth receives it  
without ending.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a philosophical lyric poem exploring the idea that we are continually becoming rather than simply being; include February fields, yellow willows, music, and the human heart.
counterfactuals.output:
**Becoming**

In February fields, the frost  
loosens its grammar underfoot;  
each furrow holds a darker word  
the thaw has not yet spoken.

Along the river, yellow willows  
lean into their first imagining—  
not leaf, not flame, but something  
on its way to both.

And music, entering the air,  
does not remain the note it was:  
it opens, vanishes, becomes  
the listening that follows.

So too the human heart—  
no finished room, no steady star,  
but a door made of arriving,  
a pulse that alters what it names.

We say *I am*, as if the world  
would let us rest inside a noun.  
Yet breath by breath, we cross ourselves,  
more bridge than destination.

Even the light is leaving  
at the instant it appears;  
even these bare fields are turning  
toward a green they cannot know.

Perhaps to live is not to be,  
but to become without conclusion—  
like willows brightening in the cold,  
like music passing through the heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an imagistic contemporary poem in three sections separated by bullets, moving from animals running through a landscape to a violin performance and finally to laundry hanging in a bright spring garden.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk, the horses break from the pines,  
black commas flung across the snowmelt.  
A fox threads the ditch. Deer lift  
through mustard grass, each body  
briefly carrying the sun.  
Even the field seems to run—  
fence posts flickering, creek water  
dragging its silver sleeve.

•

Under one white light, the violinist  
raises a small weather to her chin.  
The bow crosses: rain, then wire,  
then a voice opening  
where no mouth is.  
Her red shoe keeps time.  
In the back row, someone closes his eyes  
and the whole room turns blue.

•

Morning clips shirts to the line—  
sleeves full of April, sheets  
bright as unmailed letters.  
Tulips hold their cups beneath them.  
A yellow dress kicks at the breeze;  
two socks revolve in their private sky.  
Beyond the hedge, bees begin  
their soft machinery,  
and every wet cloth shines  
as if the garden had learned to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, meditative poem about the desire to feel wholly alive and undivided, ending with the paradoxical line “What gives you life’s the thing that kills.”
counterfactuals.output:
I want the blood to speak one language—  
no border drawn between the wound and wonder,  
no hidden room where half a self  
keeps watch while half goes wandering.

Let every nerve become a listening root,  
each breath a gate unlatched to weather;  
let grief arrive without disguise,  
and joy strike deep enough to sever  
the ancient knot of fear from flame.

I have been many things at once:  
the thirst, the cup, the hand that trembles;  
the locked door and the turning key,  
the scattered glass that still remembers  
its first, unbroken face of sand.

To live entire: not safe, not spared,  
but gathered into one bright peril—  
to meet the world with nothing numb,  
to wear the mortal as the feral  
rose wears its fragrance into dusk.

Perhaps the whole heart must be pierced  
by what it chooses, what it wills;  
perhaps the soul is most complete  
where it is broken open—still,

What gives you life’s the thing that kills.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you produce an experimental free-verse poem where everything seems to pour, shake, ripple, and run together—light, blood, wood, weather, thought, and the self?
counterfactuals.output:
**Weather for a Body Without Edges**

Morning spills its coins through the blinds  
and the floor drinks brightness  
board by board—  
the house loosening into grain,  
grain into river,  
river into the long yellow nerve of noon.

Under my skin, a red weather  
shakes its small bells.  
I lift one hand:  
five tributaries tremble  
toward whatever they touch.

The table remembers being rain.  
Its knots widen, dark eyes  
rippling under the varnish.  
A cup pours its silence  
into my mouth.  
My mouth runs over.

Outside, wind worries the trees  
until wood becomes gesture,  
gesture becomes green noise,  
and every leaf is a thought  
unable to stay thought.

Clouds drag their wet sleeves  
across the roofs.  
Chimneys dissolve upward.  
Birds leak from one shape  
into another.

I try to say *I*  
but the word will not hold—  
it shivers into light,  
light into blood,  
blood into the chair beneath me,  
the chair into forest,  
the forest into storm—

and now the storm is indoors,  
turning the pages of my ribs,  
pouring dusk through every sentence.

Nothing keeps its border.

The mirror runs down the wall.  
My face follows.  
My name, shaken loose,  
floats briefly in the floorboards  
then darkens with the grain.

By evening, even gravity is water.

The moon tips its pale bucket.  
The roads gleam and wander.  
Houses drift through their own windows.  
I step outside—

or the outside steps through me—

and all at once  
weather, timber, vein, idea,  
all the bright broken vessels  
emptying into one another,

not vanishing,

no—

becoming the pour.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
